item.title: JJ McCarthy considered 'unpredictable' as Vikings hand starting QB role to Kyler Murray: report
item.description: A source told CBS Sports that J.J. McCarthy was seen as "unpredictable" within the Minnesota Vikings, factoring into the quick decision to name Kyler Murray starter.
item.content:encoded:
It may not have come as a surprise to people that Minnesota Vikings head coach Kevin O’Connell quickly named Kyler Murray the starting quarterback of his offense over J.J. McCarthy, the team’s 2024 first-round selection.

But a recent report indicates that it’s more than just what happened on the training camp practice field between Murray and McCarthy that may have factored into such a quick decision.

It was last summer when some within the Vikings organization were concerned that McCarthy, who missed his entire rookie season due to a knee injury and struggled with consistency in 2025, was "unpredictable," according to CBS Sports.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE SPORTS COVERAGE ON FOXNEWS.COM

In fact, some believed that Max Brosmer, who was an undrafted free agent added to the quarterbacks room, should’ve been the one under center for Minnesota in Week 1.

That wasn’t the case, but the Vikings made it quite known after watching McCarthy complete 57.6% of his passes and throw 11 touchdowns to 12 interceptions across 10 games – Minnesota went 6-4 over that span – they were in the quarterback market this offseason.

KYLER MURRAY AND JJ MCCARTHY GIVE WILDLY DIFFERENT ANSWERS ABOUT THEIR VIKINGS QB ROOM DYNAMIC

"A franchise quarterback is supposed to be the stability piece of a franchise, like you know what you’re getting every day. But with J.J., you weren’t sure which version you were going to get," the source said to the outlet. "I think he’s just still so young and may not have understood yet what that position fully entails and things like the consistency and day-to-day commitment."

The Vikings landed Murray, the former No. 1 overall pick of the Arizona Cardinals, who moved on from him after a roller-coaster tenure in the desert.

And before they faced the New York Giants for their first preseason bout of the 2026 NFL season, the Vikings came right out and named Murray their starter.

So, what exactly does McCarthy’s future hold as he’s in Year 3 and serving as a backup now? One defensive coach told CBS Sports that "he is talented," though he needs to "learn how to manage a game and not do too much and not do more than what’s required of him." If that happens, perhaps the Vikings, or a different team, can trust him in a starting role.

But that’s the thing: is it too soon to discuss McCarthy playing for a different team already? The Vikings do have a new GM, Nolan Teasley, who is not tied to McCarthy’s selection. That was Kwesi Adofo-Mensah, whom the Vikings fired this past offseason.

There’s also the injury factor that hasn’t allowed McCarthy to really get going after winning a national championship with Michigan and being a top 10 pick to the Vikings. The sample size is only 10 games, and though his quarterback rating was the second worst among signal callers with more than 155 pass attempts, there were some flashes of good quarterback play.

And then there’s his age. McCarthy is only 23 years old and can still grow and develop within the position. But he still has tons to prove.

The only problem is Murray, who has proven more in his career thus far, is someone O’Connell trusts more right now with his offense. And O’Connell knows what works — just look at what he did with Sam Darnold in 2024 while McCarthy was injured throughout the season. Darnold went on to revive his career and ultimately win the Super Bowl with the Seattle Seahawks this past season.

One can’t blame Vikings fans if they believe O’Connell can revitalize Murray’s career, but they certainly will hope so after the announcement was made. Meanwhile, McCarthy will have to keep working and wait for that next moment to prove himself.

In his first preseason work with the Vikings on Saturday against the Giants, McCarthy went 4-of-7 for 34 yards with a sack. Carson Wentz , who is battling for the backup role behind Murray as well, went 6-of-11 for 56 yards with one touchdown pass to Myles Price.

Murray played the opening series for the Vikings, connecting on two of his three pass attempts, including a third-and-7 strike to keep a scoring drive alive.

item.title: Cardinals rookie makes MLB history by hitting a home run in each of his first three career plate appearances
item.description: St. Louis Cardinals rookie outfielder Joshua Báez made Major League Baseball history by hitting a home run in each of his first three plate appearances.
item.content:encoded:
St. Louis Cardinals rookie Joshua Báez’s first career game in the big leagues was something out of a movie.

Báez made Major League Baseball history by hitting a home run in each of his first three plate appearances in the Cardinals' game against the Chicago Cubs on Saturday afternoon at Wrigley Field. The 23-year-old wasted no time in his first-ever at bat, as he blasted the first pitch he saw in his major league career 450 feet to dead center field for a two-run homer to give the Cardinals a 3-0 lead.

Báez pummeled Cubs starter Matt Boyd’s 93-mph fastball and sent the Cardinals’ dugout into a frenzy. The rookie rounded the bases with a smile on his face the entire time.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE SPORTS COVERAGE ON FOXNEWS.COM

His second home run of the day came in the fourth inning, once again off Boyd. Báez worked the count full and then hammered Boyd's 78-mph changeup 382 feet into the left-field seats to give the Cardinals a 4-3 lead.

Báez's third home run also came off Boyd, this time off an 83-mph slider on the outside of the plate. The electrifying rookie hammered the ball 368 feet into the right-field seats for a two-run home run, giving the Cardinals a 6-3 lead. The Cardinals' dugout was in disbelief, with multiple players in awe of Báez's historic feat.

The right-handed hitter homered to all three fields on three different pitches in his first three plate appearances of his career. Báez homered off a fastball in his first at-bat to center field, a changeup to left field in his second at-bat, and a slider to right field in his third at-bat. It was a remarkable display of power in his first career game.

In his fourth at-bat, he proved he was human, as he just hit a line out to Cubs left fielder Ian Happ. At the time of this writing, the Cardinals had an 8-4 lead over the Cubs in the ninth inning.

Báez, who led Triple-A in home runs before being called up on Saturday, was batting fifth in the order and playing left field. In Triple-A, the Boston native was putting up massive numbers, hitting .256 with 34 home runs, 90 RBI and 21 stolen bases in 103 games.

The Cardinals drafted him in the second round of the 2021 MLB Draft out of high school. The team hopes he can join JJ Wetherholt, Jordan Walker and Alec Burleson to form a young core the team can build around for a long time.

The Cardinals were not expected to compete this season but have surprised many as they entered Saturday at 61-61 and just 3.5 games back of the Arizona Diamondbacks and Philadelphia Phillies for the final Wild Card spot in the National League.

item.title: Trump backs Republican challenger to oust Letitia James amid ongoing mortgage fraud feud
item.description: President Donald Trump endorsed Saritha Komatireddy to challenge Letitia James, calling the New York attorney general the "WORST" in the country.
item.content:encoded:
New York Attorney General Letitia James has drawn a Trump-backed challenger, with President Donald Trump throwing his "complete and total endorsement" behind Republican Saritha Komatireddy in a bid to oust his longtime political foe.

"It is my Great Honor to endorse America First Patriot, Saritha Komatireddy, who is running to be the next Attorney General of the once wonderful State of New York," Trump wrote in a Friday Truth Social post. "Between Kathy Hochul and the Most Corrupt Attorney General in the Country, Letitia James, it has gone to HELL!"

Trump’s endorsement of Komatireddy, who he nominated to U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of New York in 2020, comes as he continues pressing for James to be prosecuted over mortgage fraud allegations, adding another front to his years-long feud with the Democratic attorney general who once took him to court.

TRUMP'S JUSTICE DEPARTMENT SUES NEW YORK, OTHER BLUE STATES OVER TUITION FOR ILLEGAL IMMIGRANTS

Trump did not mince his words in his criticism of James, who successfully sued Trump and The Trump Organization in 2022, accusing them of fraudulently inflating the value of assets on financial statements to obtain more favorable loans.

An appeals court later wiped out the nearly $465 million financial penalty against Trump, ruling the massive disgorgement award violated the Constitution’s prohibition on excessive fines.

"Letitia 'Peekaboo' James, is considered by many to be the WORST Attorney General in our Country. She is a Complete and Total Disaster, who tried running against Kathy Hochul for Governor, and got less than 1% of the Vote in the Polls, and QUIT, taking many innocent suckers down with her," Trump wrote. "She then went back to her WITCH HUNT against your favorite President, (ME!), and others, yet Murder and other Violent Crime is RAGING OUT OF CONTROL in New York, as People and Businesses flee, in Record Numbers, to other States!"

He contrasted James to Komatireddy, touting her qualifications as Drug Enforcement Administration chief of staff, a former federal prosecutor, and that she clerked for Brett Kavanaugh, who went on to become a Supreme Court justice.

"On the other hand, as your next Attorney General, Saritha Komatireddy will fight tirelessly to Ensure LAW AND ORDER, Grow our Economy, Champion our Law Enforcement and First Responders, Support our Military/Veterans, Advance Election Integrity, Keep our Border SECURE, Stop Migrant Crime, Uphold our Constitution, and Defend our always under siege Second Amendment," Trump wrote.

TRUMP MAY HAVE ENDORSED DARLINE GRAHAM, BUT GOP SENATE HOPEFULS AREN’T BACKING DOWN

Komatireddy, who has been outspoken against James' handling of the state's fraud investigations, thanked Trump for his endorsement.

"I was honored to be nominated to be a federal judge by the President in 2020 and I’m honored to receive his endorsement today. I’m working hard to win the support of all New Yorkers and defeat Letitia James this November," Komatireddy wrote on X.

Fox News Digital reached out to James' campaign for comment.

item.title: Courtney Love reveals secret health crisis that nearly killed her: 'My body just exploded'
item.description: Courtney Love shared that her body "just exploded" during a secret health crisis that left her near death, losing all her hair and dropping to 100 pounds.
item.content:encoded:
Courtney Love is revealing a health battle she kept private for years.

The Hole singer, 62, shared an update about her long-awaited new album, explaining that the record took shape during a period when she was frequently hospitalized and believed it could be her final work.

"I went to England in 2019 and when I went there, you know, my body just exploded," Love said in an Instagram video. "It just exploded. And I was in hospitals a lot. I almost died, I lost all my hair. I was about 100 pounds. And they told me I was going to die, and I didn’t believe them."

KURT COBAIN AND COURTNEY LOVE ATTEMPTED TO ESCAPE 'CRAZINESS' OF FAME

Love did not identify the illness or illnesses she was battling, but said she ultimately recovered after refusing to accept the prognosis she had been given.

The singer connected that determination to a memory from childhood, describing a tendency to challenge what adults told her was true.

"When I was a kid — and I think this record is about this — I used to pattern interrupt the adults," she said. "They’d tell me red was blue, and then I’d see blue, but blue was blue, so now that I gaslight myself that maybe they were right, and red was blue, and then I would see purple, and my head would explode. Like f---ing cope with that s---, right?"

She continued, "I never really lost my ability to see that… red was red. Despite them telling me that red was blue. And so, when they said ‘you’re going to die,’ I just didn’t believe them. And somehow, I got better. I’m healthy, which is amazing."

"I just wasn’t public about being sick. I don’t want to be public. I’m fine now."

The singer said she wants to return to the road and perform again, describing music as essential to her well-being.

Her new album appears to have emerged directly from the period in which she was fighting to recover.

In an Instagram caption accompanying her video, Love explained that when she began making the record, she believed it might be her last.

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR THE ENTERTAINMENT NEWSLETTER

"I wanted to give you an update on my record. When I made it, I believed this was my last record so I made the record I always wanted to make. I was in the hospital mostly but when I wasn’t all I did was write & record it."

Love also thanked those who worked with her while she was dealing with what she described as trauma.

The project would mark a significant return for Love, who has not released an album since Hole’s 2010 "Nobody’s Daughter."

She closed her message by asking fans for patience as she prepares to return to public life.

item.title: Everyday habit linked to dramatically lower risk of dying from heart disease
item.description: Stair climbing was linked to a 39% lower risk of dying from cardiovascular disease, according to an analysis of more than 480,000 participants.
item.content:encoded:
A simple daily habit may be linked to a dramatically lower risk of premature death, particularly from heart disease — no gym membership required.

People who climbed stairs had a 39% lower risk of dying from cardiovascular disease and a 24% lower risk of dying from any cause than those who didn’t, according to an analysis led by researchers at the University of East Anglia and Norfolk and Norwich University Hospital.

DAD SUFFERS HEART ATTACK DAYS BEFORE DAUGHTER'S WEDDING — THEN DOCTORS MAKE SURE HE WALKS HER DOWN THE AISLE

People who climbed the stairs were less likely to develop major cardiovascular conditions such as heart attack, stroke and heart failure, UEA further reported.

"Cardiovascular disease is the leading cause of death worldwide — with cases nearly doubling between 1990 and 2019," Vassilios Vassiliou, from UEA’s Norwich Medical School, said in a news release.

After reviewing nearly 1,900 studies, the researchers analyzed data from more than 480,000 people across nine studies, which had a median follow-up period of 14 years. The participants included healthy people and those with a history of heart problems, between the ages of 35 and 84.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS

The findings show an association between stair climbing and lower mortality risk, but do not prove that taking the stairs directly causes people to live longer.

Stair climbing is a simple but powerful form of exercise because it requires the body to repeatedly work against gravity. The generally low-impact activity engages multiple muscle groups while providing both cardiovascular and strength-building benefits.

One large study included in the analysis suggested that climbing about six flights of stairs per day may offer the greatest benefit, though researchers said more work is needed to determine the optimal amount.

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER

"Some of the studies we looked at showed that the more stairs climbed, the greater the health benefits," said UEA’s Norwich Medical School researcher Sophie Paddock. "But even small changes had a measurable impact."

According to Vassiliou, more than a quarter of adults worldwide fail to meet recommended activity levels. A sedentary lifestyle, smoking, poor dietary habits and obesity all contribute to cardiovascular disease.

Climbing stairs is a cost-free form of exercise people can fit into their day at home, work and in public places and is a good option for people who don't have much time or easy access to exercise, the researchers said.

"Even brief bursts of physical activity have beneficial health impacts, and short bouts of stair climbing should be an achievable target to integrate into daily routines," Paddock said.

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

The researchers cautioned that stair climbing may not be appropriate for everyone, particularly people with mobility issues or joint conditions.

They published their findings in the American Journal of Cardiovascular Drugs.

item.title: Dolly Parton’s ongoing health battle forces country legend to miss major Dollywood event
item.description: Dolly Parton appeared virtually at Dollywood's new roller coaster opening after her Nashville doctor grounded her travel over dizziness and dehydration.
item.content:encoded:
Country music icon Dolly Parton was forced to miss a major Dollywood event Friday after her doctor advised her to stay in Nashville because of continued "health issues."

The 80-year-old "9 to 5" singer was expected to appear in person at the Tennessee theme park for the opening of its new NightFlight Expedition roller coaster, but she ultimately joined the celebration virtually after her doctor told her not to travel.

"I’m still in Nashville, and I’m sorry about that," Parton told the crowd during a video appearance at the event, according to video shared by the Knoxville News Sentinel.

DOLLY PARTON'S SISTER OFFERS HEALTH UPDATE ON COUNTRY ICON AFTER FANS WORRY OVER HER CALL FOR PRAYERS

"I’m supposed to be there in person, like we planned," she continued. "Now I’ve told you before, all my fans, that I have had a few little health issues. And sometimes I get a little dizzy, and I get dehydrated."

"And I’m dehydrated," Parton, who appeared on-screen wearing fairy wings, told the crowd. "And so my Nashville doctor clipped my wings, saying ‘you ain’t traveling this week.’"

DOLLY PARTON UNABLE TO WRITE NEW SONGS AFTER LOSING HUSBAND OF NEARLY 60 YEARS

"So I guess if your doctor tells you, ‘you ain’t traveling this week,’ you ain’t traveling this week," she continued, explaining that she likes keeping her fans "in the loop" and had promised to update them "on everything."

Fox News Digital has reached out to Parton for comment.

LEANN RIMES CANCELS CONCERTS DUE TO SEVERE ILLNESS, SAYS SHE IS 'TRULY HEARTBROKEN'

Parton’s absence comes as she continues to recover from health problems that have forced her to scale back some of her performance plans.

In May, the country legend announced that she was canceling her planned Las Vegas residency, which had already been postponed from 2025 to September 2026 because of health concerns.

"I'm here to give you an update on a few things going on in my life," Parton said in the video at the time. "First, it is concerning my health. And I have some good news and a little bad news. But the good news is, I'm responding really well to meds and treatments, and I'm improving every day."

LIKE WHAT YOU’RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

As for the bad news, Parton acknowledged that she wasn't yet physically ready to perform at the level she expected from herself at the time.

"It's going to take me a little while before I'm up to stage-performance level, because some of the meds and treatments make me a little bit swimmy-headed, as my grandma used to say," she quipped. "And, of course I can't be dizzy, carrying around banjos, guitars, and such on five-inch heels... not to mention all those heavy rhinestone outfits, the big hair, my big personality."

Parton has previously discussed problems involving kidney stones, while also saying her immune and digestive systems had gotten "out of whack" and were being treated. She has repeatedly emphasized that she is improving.

"I have great doctors, and I'm doing really well, and they assure me that everything I have is treatable," she said. "So I'm going with that, and I just want you to know I thank you for standing by me and that I will always love you."

item.title: Cardinals top pick Jeremiyah Love out for a least a week after suffering preseason injury, coach says
item.description: Tyler Allgeier steps into the starting RB role as the Arizona Cardinals manage key injuries to Jeremiyah Love and veteran James Conner this week.
item.content:encoded:
The Arizona Cardinals will be without the No. 3 overall pick in the 2026 NFL Draft for at least a week.

Head coach Mike LaFleur said Saturday that running back Jeremiyah Love suffered an ankle injury during the team’s preseason game against the Las Vegas Raiders on Thursday. Love, despite not having much concern following the game, came into the building on Friday sore.

"He was in great spirits, even Friday," LaFleur said. "But we'll keep him out this week as we let it heal. So, a little bit more sore than we were anticipating."

CLICK HERE FOR MORE SPORTS COVERAGE ON FOXNEWS.COM

When asked how Love’s injury could impact his Week 1 status, LaFleur declined to look further than Saturday’s practice.

"This week and then we'll kind of go from there and reevaluate," LaFleur said. "Honestly, all the focus is on August 15th, Saturday. Here we are in our Tempe block (of practice). We'll kind of reevaluate going into next week. But he will be out this week."

LaFleur said Love will not play in the team’s second preseason game against the Dallas Cowboys next Saturday. Love recorded 11 carries for 58 yards and three catches for 14 yards in the Cardinals’ first preseason game.

SIGN UP TO GET THE LATEST SPORTS NEWS

With Love out, Tyler Allgeier will step into the starting role with Bam Knight and Corey Kiner backing him up. Veteran running back James Conner has not yet participated in 11-on-11 drills as he recovers from a right foot injury that forced him to miss 14 games last season.

Unfortunately for the Cardinals, Love is not the only rookie who sustained an injury in the team’s first preseason game. Second-round pick Chase Bisontis, who was in contention for the starting right guard position, tore the MCL in his left knee.

LaFleur said Bisontis will be placed on injured reserve, delivering a huge blow to the Cardinals' offensive line. He will undergo surgery on the injured knee.

"He'll be out for a good amount of time, if not the whole year," LaFleur said. "Sucks for him. Always think about the player first. Sucks for the Cardinals too, He's a good player but more importantly you hate it for the player."

item.title: Bernie-backed California House candidate called DEI a ‘social justice-driven duty,’ embraced activist role
item.description: Bernie Sanders-backed California candidate Randy Villegas promoted DEI as a "social justice-driven duty" in his academic writings on community colleges.
item.content:encoded:
A Bernie Sanders-backed California congressional candidate who touts his career as an educator has used the classroom and academia to push diversity, equity and inclusion (DEI) initiatives and activist groups, according to his own writings and reports on his work with students.

Randy Villegas is taking on Republican Rep. David Valadao in California’s 22nd Congressional District in a high-stakes Central Valley showdown that could help determine control of the House.

Democrats have made the seat a top pickup target as the nonpartisan Cook Political Report rates the district a "toss-up" and gives the district a razor-thin D+1 partisan lean.

Villegas, a political science professor at College of the Sequoias and Visalia school board trustee, co-authored a 2022 academic paper arguing that DEI is central to the mission of community college educators and describing it as a "social justice-driven duty."

The paper, titled "A Commitment to Teaching, Learning, and Student Advocacy: Community College Careers," was published by the American Political Science Association as a chapter in Strategies for Navigating Graduate School and Beyond.

"At the heart of community college teaching is diversity, equity, and inclusion, and culturally responsive teaching," Villegas wrote. "Community colleges commit to teaching excellence and to a social justice-driven duty to accessibility. Most community colleges have similar institutional characteristics as a result. For example, community colleges are open access institutions. This means that all students are accepted."

COAST GUARD ENDING RACE-BASED ADMISSIONS FOR OFFICER COMMISSIONING PROGRAM UNDER TRUMP DEI CRACKDOWN

Villegas and his co-authors framed diversity and inclusion as a responsibility that extended beyond campus, writing that "a commitment to diversity and inclusion expands from the classroom to the communities in which students live" and arguing that students’ "social and economic realities" should also shape course design.

While the paper pre-dates President Donald Trump’s push to eliminate DEI mandates across the federal government and education system, it sheds light on Villegas’ views on DEI and social justice in higher education.

In his dissertation, "Voices from the Valley of Vulnerability," written for the University of California, Santa Cruz, Villegas identifies himself as a "former community organizer and scholar activist" and makes the case that activism can be part of his scholarly work.

He bats away concerns that activism could affect academic objectivity, arguing that his activism gave him access to information and that his identity and life experiences made his research stronger. He cites scholar Zepeda-Millán, who argued that researchers’ "biases can actually be assets."

MICHIGAN SENATE CANDIDATE ABDUL EL-SAYED DODGES QUESTION ON WHETHER HE STILL SUPPORTS DEFUNDING THE POLICE

Throughout the paper, Villegas described taking part in grassroots activism that included organizing May Day demonstrations, protesting outside an immigrant detention center and working with community groups to advocate for far-left causes.

He argued that schools often failed to sufficiently engage students in politics, describing educational institutions as "anti-political" while praising community organizations for "actively politicizing and socializing youth" and empowering them to become "agents of change."

That push to turn students into political activists went beyond his academia research. In 2018, Villegas helped lead the Central Valley Freedom Summer (CVFS), a program that connected students with community organizations for voter outreach, civic engagement and grassroots organizing. Participants worked on issues including LGBTQ rights, immigration, environmental justice and racial inequality while conducting voter-registration and turnout efforts. Among those groups that teamed up with CVFS was Jakara Movement. In 2020, the group launched a campaign seeking the removal of a statue of Mahatma Gandhi, citing what it described as Gandhi’s "history of anti-Blackness and racism," Breitbart reported.

Some CVFS graduates went on to launch activist groups of their own, including LOUD for Tomorrow, a self-described "queer and trans BIPOC youth-led" organization that has hosted youth drag events across the Central Valley.

600 GROUPS WITH $2B IN REVENUE MOBILIZE 3,000 MAY DAY PROTESTS IN A 'RED-BLUE' ALLIANCE, PROBE FINDS

"Randy Villegas was cooked up in a lab to be the radical left's perfect woke freak. The only thing he cares about is political power and his far-left agenda," Republican National Committee spokesperson Nick Poche told Fox News Digital.

Meanwhile, Villegas did not respond to Fox News Digital’s questions about his statements that educators also wear the hat of a "social activist." Instead, a spokesperson made remarks about incumbent Valadao.

"David Valadao ripped away healthcare and food assistance from Valley families to hand his billionaire buddies a tax break," the spokesperson said in an email. "These desperate attacks won’t hide his toxic record, or the domestic abusers bankrolling his campaign."

The comments appear to refer to Valadao voting in favor of President Donald Trump’s "One Big Beautiful Bill", a sweeping tax and spending package that included roughly $1 trillion in Medicaid cuts. Democrats have argued the cuts could cause tens of thousands of people in Valadao’s heavily Medi-Cal-dependent district to lose coverage.

Fox News Digital reached out to Valadao's chief of staff and communications director for comment, as well as Villegas' campaign for clarification on the allegation that "domestic abusers" are financing Valadao's campaign.

All three traditional Pixel 11 models now start with 256GB of storage. Google also carries Pixelsnap magnetic wireless charging into the Pixel 11 lineup, with Qi2 support and faster wireless charging that can reach up to 25W on compatible models. Pixelsnap lets you snap on compatible chargers, stands, grips and other magnetic accessories.

Then there is the Pixel 11 Pro Fold. Google made it almost 10% lighter and about 1 millimeter thinner than the Pixel 10 Pro Fold. A redesigned hinge, new back material and stronger outer display also make it three times more durable than last year's Fold, according to Google's testing. That gives the Pixel 11 family a clearer reason to upgrade beyond AI alone. Google has changed the cameras, durability and charging experience while refining the physical design.

Google is also trying to make switching from an iPhone less painful. Quick Share on Pixel can now send and receive photos and videos with iPhones and MacBooks, while Google says your photos and group chats can move over when you switch.

All four Pixel 11 phones are available for preorder now, including the Google Pixel 11, Google Pixel 11 Pro, Google Pixel 11 Pro XL and Google Pixel 11 Pro Fold. They officially go on sale August 20.

FBI HELPS TAKE DOWN AI PHISHING RING

Google is taking another step toward making Gemini feel less like an app you open and more like something that can help across your phone. Gemini can now handle multistep tasks across more than 40 apps. Pixel 11 can also surface information based on what you are doing. For example, if a friend messages you about an upcoming trip, a card can appear with your booking information and flight status. Pixel can also suggest actions based on your conversation. If you are discussing dinner plans, for example, it may offer a prompt to make a reservation. It can suggest adding an event to Calendar or saving a location to Maps.

Google also introduced Rambler, a Gemini-powered voice input feature. It cleans up natural speech as it transcribes you. That means filler words such as "um" and "ah" do not have to end up in your finished message. That could be one of those small features you quickly start using every day.

Much of this is powered by Google's new Tensor G6 processor. Google says Tensor G6 can process on-device AI tasks up to 3.5 times faster while using up to 3.5 times less energy than the previous generation under its testing.

Google also introduced Sign To Text, which lets Pixel understand American Sign Language through the camera. Users can sign to write, chat or prompt Gemini from the keyboard. Google says the feature can recognize one-handed and two-handed signing along with facial expressions for grammar and tone. It is available for ASL now, with more sign languages planned.

One of my favorite ideas from the event is Magic Capture. Instead of making you concentrate on hitting the shutter at exactly the right second, Magic Capture can analyze around 400 frames during a typical session. It then delivers carefully timed 12-megapixel photos. The feature can also automatically crop or unblur an image. At the same time, it saves video without making you switch camera modes. That could come in handy with kids, pets or anything else that refuses to pose for you.

The hardware gets an upgrade too. Pixel 11 has a new 48-megapixel main sensor that Google says delivers 56% more light sensitivity than Pixel 10. Its 5x telephoto camera can reach 30x Super Zoom. Meanwhile, Pixel 11 Pro and Pro XL get an upgraded 48-megapixel telephoto camera. Google says its larger sensor provides 30% more light sensitivity. The Pro phones can reach up to 120x Pro Zoom.

Google says the new Instant Night Sight is four times faster, helping Pixel capture low-light photos without requiring you to hold the phone still as long. There is also a new Camera Looks feature. It lets you choose a visual style before taking the photo. You can select a default look or customize additional styles to suit the shot. If the camera is your biggest reason for upgrading a phone, you may also want to compare the new Pixels with our current top Android phones of 2026 at cyberguy.com.

Remember when phones had little notification lights? Google is bringing that idea back in a much more noticeable way. Pixel 11 Pro and Pixel 11 Pro XL introduce HiLight. Colored LED lights around the camera flash can glow while the phone is face down.

For example, HiLight uses different patterns to show when Gemini is listening, thinking or responding. You can also assign colors to important contacts so an incoming call gives you a visual clue about who is calling. Google says message notifications from favorite contacts are among the capabilities planned for HiLight later.

I like the thinking here. Phones are very good at pulling us back onto the screen. A quick visual signal could give you useful information without demanding your full attention. The Pixel 11 Pro Fold gets HiLight as well.

With Gemini getting access to more context on your phone, privacy was an obvious question at the event. Google says Pixel gives users visibility into what AI is doing and controls over how their data is used. You can also turn AI features on or off.

Google highlighted several security protections built into Pixel 11. The phone can automatically block many spam calls and texts while warning you about messages or calls that may be scams. Google is also promising seven years of automatic security updates. An upgraded security chip is designed to help protect personal information stored on the phone.

Pixel Watch 5 may be the device I would watch most closely after launch. Google upgraded its GPS and says route tracking can be twice as accurate as previous Pixel Watch generations in difficult environments. The watch also gets 50% more RAM and a faster processor compared with Pixel Watch 4. Then there is Google Health. Pixel Watch 5 introduces Health Guardian features that look for longer-term changes in your wellness. These include monthly summaries involving blood pressure trends, sleep breathing quality and insulin resistance trends. Google says these features are designed for general wellness and are not intended to diagnose or treat medical conditions.

The headline safety feature is Breathing Emergency Detection. It uses the watch's sensors and on-device AI to look for a severe, persistent drop in oxygen saturation. If the wearer becomes unresponsive, the watch can automatically call emergency services and transmit the person's location. There is an important catch for U.S. buyers. Breathing Emergency Detection is currently available on Pixel Watch 4 and Pixel Watch 5 in select European countries. It is not currently available in the United States. Google says it plans to expand the feature to more countries.

Pixel Watch 5 is available for preorder now and starts at $399 for the 41mm model and $429 for the 45mm version. The watches go on sale August 20.

Google is officially entering the finder-tag business. Pixel Tag is a small tracker for things such as keys, wallets or luggage. It connects to Google's Find Hub network, which includes more than one billion Android devices. That network can help locate an item when your own phone is no longer nearby. When you are close to the tag, Ultra-Wideband with Bluetooth Channel Sounding can provide distance and directional guidance on compatible devices. You can also make the Pixel Tag play a sound. Interestingly, the button on the tag works in reverse too. Press it and you can ring your phone.

Google says the replaceable battery lasts more than one year. The tag carries an IP67 water and dust resistance rating. You can also share a Pixel Tag with up to 10 people. Security matters with any location tracker. Google says Android phones automatically warn you if an unknown tag appears to be traveling with you.

We have covered Google's expanding location tools before. You can read more about Find Hub and Google's Android security protections.

Pixel Tag costs $29 for one or $99 for a four-pack. It is not available for preorder yet. Google says it goes on sale November 11.

WHAT A SCAMMER SEES THE MOMENT THEY GOOGLE YOUR NAME

Google did not replace the Pixel Buds Pro 2. Instead, it announced new software features and a new Olive finish. Google says an upgraded Active Noise Cancellation feature can compensate when the fit or seal changes, helping maintain noise cancellation while you are moving.

Another clever feature connects the Buds with Pixel Watch. Later this year, your Buds will automatically pause audio if your Pixel Watch senses that you have fallen asleep. Google also says Live Translate improvements are coming to Pixel Buds Pro 2 and Pixel Buds 2a later this fall. Pixel Buds Pro 2 are also getting the new Olive color to complement this year's Pixel devices.

The Pixel Buds Pro 2 are available now, with the new Olive color joining the lineup.

Google could have spent its Pixel 11 launch talking mainly about faster processors and brighter displays. Instead, some of the most interesting changes focus on reducing how much attention your devices demand. Magic Capture could make it easier to get the photo without experiencing the entire moment through your screen. HiLight could tell you whether a call matters before you pick up your phone.

I am also watching the Pixel Watch 5 closely. A watch that can automatically call for help during certain breathing emergencies could become an important safety tool. However, U.S. buyers need to know that feature is not available here yet. Pixel Tag feels overdue, especially given the size of Google's Find Hub network. Still, proactive Gemini may be the biggest shift. Your phone can increasingly use context from your apps and conversations to decide what information might help you next. That could save time, but it also makes understanding your privacy settings more important.

How much should your phone know about what you are doing in order to predict what you need next? Would you welcome that kind of help or rather have Gemini wait until you ask? Let us know by writing to us at Cyberguy.com

item.title: Trump’s $100K Wall Street Truth access draws lawsuit as expert warns it ‘raises the stakes’ on ethics
item.description: President Donald Trump's Truth Social API charges Wall Street firms up to $100,000 monthly for early access to his market-moving posts on tariffs and policy updates.
item.content:encoded:
President Donald Trump was sued in federal court this week over a Truth Social service that sells Wall Street traders early access to his posts on tariffs, war and other market-moving policy — for a six-figure price.

The lawsuit was filed by the Freedom of the Press Foundation and news outlet The Intercept in New York federal court on Wednesday.

According to court documents obtained by Fox News Digital, the plaintiffs allege the Truth API service offered by the Trump Media and Technology Group (TMTG) is in direct violation of the Constitution and that information released by Trump should be available to everyone simultaneously.

Trump’s deputy chief of staff Daniel Scavino and his executive assistant Natalie J. Harp are also named as defendants.

TRUTH SOCIAL PLAN TO SELL EARLY ACCESS TO TRUMP POSTS ‘MAKES ME WANT TO PUKE,’ CNBC REPORTER FUMES

The monthly subscription was rolled out on Aug. 1 and charges Wall Street firms an eye-watering monthly fee of $60,000 to $100,000 in exchange for early access to market-moving posts from Truth Social accounts with large followings, including Trump’s own account with 13 million followers.

"Trump had a right to say whatever he wants, but he can’t sell access to official statements through a private business while he uses his public office to undermine the Freedom of Information Act, the Presidential Records Act and virtually every other mechanism for transparency," Seth Stern, chief of advocacy at the Freedom of the Press Foundation, said in a statement to Fox News Digital.

TMTG previously said in a press release that the feed of commercial data will be available to subscribers "within milliseconds," and is expected to provide continuous 24/7 coverage and includes a historical archive of posts dating back to 2022."

TRUMP BET TARIFFS WOULD BRING BACK AMERICAN FACTORY JOBS. NEW REPORT SAYS IT DIDN'T WORK

Trump has previously used Truth Social as a method of direct communication with the public regarding market-sensitive information, including providing updates on the Iran war or newly implemented tariffs.

"Markets already move on Truth Social posts," Kevin McGurn, interim CEO of TMTG, said in a statement. "Truth API delivers a direct, licensed, real-time feed of the platform's most market-moving Truths while advancing our strategy to monetize proprietary assets through a high-margin, recurring revenue stream. As adoption grows, we expect Truth API to become a meaningful, ongoing source of revenue for the company, creating lasting value for shareholders."

The lawsuit aims to block Trump’s White House from posting official government announcements solely on Truth Social, with the plaintiffs alleging the service violates the First Amendment right to equal access to the president’s comments and Fifth Amendment prohibitions barring unreasonable conditions for government resources.

WHITE HOUSE CONDEMNS STAFFER ACCUSED OF BETTING ON TRUMP SPEECH AS A 'DISGRACE'

Trump serves as the largest shareholder of Trump Media, accounting for 40% of its share ownership.

The plaintiffs also took aim at a separate agreement between Trump Media and Trump that provides Truth Social with six hours of exclusive access to his posts before they can be shared on other platforms, asking the court to bar Trump from "posting official government information exclusively" on his own website.

The offering has sparked ethical questions among watchdogs, with media expert Kaivan Shroff telling Fox News Digital Trump’s financial stake in the company could harm his defense in the case.

"Trump’s financial stake matters legally here because it gives the plaintiffs a much stronger argument that the alleged preferential treatment isn’t serving some legitimate government purpose, but instead a private financial interest," Shroff said, adding, "The ownership stake doesn’t make the arrangement unconstitutional by itself, but it makes the private financial benefit much harder to dismiss as merely incidental. And therefore that weakens the defense that there is some legitimate government interest in this practice at all."

However, former state attorney Dave Aronberg believes Trump's ownership in the company is not the plaintiffs' primary hurdle in the case — it's the Constitution.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE OF MEDIA AND CULTURE

"President Trump’s ownership stake itself isn't necessarily the smoking gun for a violation, but it certainly strengthens the plaintiffs’ argument that government action and the president’s private financial interests have become unusually intertwined," Aronberg told Fox News Digital.

"The biggest challenge for the plaintiffs is the substantive issue of whether the Constitution requires essentially simultaneous access to an official presidential communication, as opposed to merely preventing the government from excluding a particular news organization altogether," he added. "The courts will separate what may be distasteful from what is unconstitutional."

Jason Mudd, CEO of Axia Public Relations, echoed the same sentiment surrounding questions about the six-figure subscription service and presidential ethics.

"This does not sit well with the electorate. Charging for faster access to a public official’s statements tells citizens their government may not be working in their interest," Mudd told Fox News Digital. "Financial advantages already exist. Turning it into a published policy with the President’s direct involvement raises the stakes and the ethics concerns."

Mudd went on to relay his own piece of advice as to how Trump Media should proceed regarding the service.

"Sunlight is the best disinfectant," Mudd said. "If this were my client, I would advise Trump Media to put real distance between the President’s financial interest and any product built on access to him and his views. Recusal is often a stronger position than litigation."

Fox News Digital reached out to the White House and Trump Media for comment but did not immediately receive a response.

item.title: Medicare and Social Security scams: Warning signs and tips
item.description: Medicare and Social Security scams use spoofed caller ID, AI-cloned voices and urgent threats to trick older adults into sharing sensitive information.
item.content:encoded:
Medicare and Social Security scams target older adults by impersonating trusted government programs and creating fear around benefits, medical coverage, or legal trouble. The scam may arrive as a phone call, text, email, social media ad, or even a message that appears to come from a benefits office. The goal is usually simple: get sensitive information, redirect money, or pressure someone into acting before they stop to verify the story.

These scams are effective because they sound official. A caller may claim your Medicare account needs to be verified, your Social Security number has been linked to fraud, or your benefits are about to be suspended. In reality, that urgency is often the biggest warning sign. Once people know the patterns, these schemes become much easier to spot and shut down. Here's how these scams work, the warning signs to watch for and the steps you can take to protect yourself or someone you love.

New! Free live CyberGuy class: Protect Your Money From Today’s Biggest Threats

Join us Saturday, August 29, at 10 AM ET for a free CyberGuy LIVE class covering five simple steps to help defend yourself against AI scams, fraud, identity theft and financial hacks. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson will explain how to set up bank alerts, strengthen your account logins, protect your phone number, freeze your credit and help secure your retirement savings against unauthorized transfers. No technical experience is needed. You’ll also receive our financial protection checklist, and every registrant will get a link to the class recording afterward.

Reserve your free spot today at CyberGuyLive.com.

IS ID.ME SAFE TO USE? WHAT YOU NEED TO KNOW

Most Medicare and Social Security scams follow a familiar script. First, the scammer pretends to represent a trusted institution. Then they introduce a problem or opportunity: a frozen benefit, a replacement card, a refund, free medical equipment, or a security issue tied to your identity. Finally, they ask for personal details, payment information, or immediate action.

A Medicare scam may ask for your Medicare number, Social Security number, or bank details to "confirm" enrollment or process a benefit. A Social Security scam may claim your Social Security number has been suspended or connected to criminal activity and must be "reactivated" right away. These claims are false. Medicare does not cold-call people for sensitive information, and the Social Security Administration does not suspend Social Security numbers or demand instant payment to resolve a problem.

Older adults are often singled out because scammers assume they are more likely to answer landlines, trust authority figures, and have retirement savings or steady benefit income. Government impersonation scams are designed to exploit those assumptions with urgency, pressure, and official-sounding language.

Scammers are also meeting seniors where they already spend time. Recent reporting has highlighted a surge in Medicare-related scam ads on Facebook, with roughly 73% of impressions from leading scam ads reaching users over 65. AI is making the problem worse too, with fraudsters using more polished scripts and, in some cases, cloned voices to sound more believable.

One common Medicare scam offers free braces, genetic testing, screenings, grocery cards, or other extra benefits in exchange for your Medicare number. Once scammers get that information, they may use it to bill Medicare fraudulently or as part of a larger identity theft scheme.

Another tactic plays on confusion around policy updates or refunds. A caller may say you overpaid for Medicare Part D, qualify for a refund, or need to verify a new Medicare card. Then they ask for your Social Security number, bank account information, or a fee to process the request. Legitimate agencies do not handle unexpected benefit issues this way.

Social Security scams usually rely on fear. A scammer may claim your Social Security number was used in a crime, your benefits are frozen, or police will be contacted unless you verify your identity or send money immediately. Some scams even blend Medicare and Social Security language to sound more official.

IS YOUR SOCIAL SECURITY NUMBER ON THE DARK WEB?

The exact script changes, but the red flags are remarkably consistent.

An unexpected call, text, or message claiming to be from Medicare or Social Security should always be treated carefully. Surprise outreach is a common trait of impersonation scams.

Scammers want people to feel rushed. They may say your benefits will end today, a refund will disappear, or your identity is at immediate risk unless you comply.

A request for your Medicare number, Social Security number, bank account details, passwords, or one-time verification codes is a major red flag, especially during an unexpected contact.

Gift cards, wire transfers, cryptocurrency, Zelle, or cash-by-mail are strong signs of fraud. Government agencies do not demand payment that way.

If someone threatens arrest, benefit cancellation, or legal action unless you act immediately, they are trying to trigger panic. That is not how legitimate agencies resolve problems.

Scammers can spoof caller ID to display a local area code or names like Medicare or Social Security. A familiar-looking number is not proof that a call is real.

The best defense is slowing the interaction down. A few simple habits can make it much harder for a scammer to catch you off guard.

Never give out your Medicare number, Social Security number, bank details, passwords, or verification codes during an unexpected call, text, or message.

If someone claims to be from Medicare or Social Security, hang up and contact the agency yourself using the number on official mail, your card, or the official website. Do not call a number provided by the person who contacted you.

Protect your Medicare number the same way you protect a credit card number. Review Medicare Summary Notices and Explanation of Benefits statements for services, equipment, or providers you do not recognize.

It helps to prepare a simple response before a suspicious call ever comes in. You can say, "I don't provide personal information over the phone. I'll call back using the official number." That gives you an easy way to end the conversation before a scammer can build more pressure.

Medicare and Social Security scams can become far more damaging once a criminal gets your Social Security number, financial information or other personal details. That information can be used to open fraudulent accounts, take over existing accounts or commit identity theft long after the original scam call or message ends. Identity theft protection can add another layer of monitoring and support if that happens.

An identity theft protection service can combine identity and financial monitoring with alerts designed to help you spot suspicious activity sooner. Depending on the plan, monitoring may cover credit activity, financial accounts, investment and retirement accounts, phone takeovers, SIM swaps, utility accounts and other areas where criminals may try to use your identity.

What identity theft protection can help with

Identity theft protection does not replace the precautions that can stop a Medicare or Social Security scam in the first place. You should still hang up on suspicious callers, independently verify benefit questions through official government channels and regularly review your Medicare and financial records. If you believe your Social Security number or other personal information has been compromised, act quickly.

Check whether your personal information may already be exposed

Scammers can be much more convincing when they already know details about you. A free exposure scan can help identify personal information connected to your email that may appear in known data breaches or on risky sites. Seeing what information may already be exposed can also help explain how a scammer knew enough about you to make a fake Medicare or Social Security message sound legitimate.

Check out my top picks for data removal services and get a free scan to find out if your personal information is already out on the web by visiting Cyberguy.com

If you already shared personal or financial information, move quickly.

Quick action can reduce the odds of broader identity theft or financial damage.

Medicare and Social Security scams keep working because they target two things older Americans understandably take seriously: their health coverage and their financial security. What concerns me most is how much more convincing these scams are becoming. Criminals can combine personal information found online with spoofed phone numbers, polished messages and even AI-generated voices to make a fake warning feel legitimate. That means the best defense is no longer trying to recognize every new scam script. It is creating one simple habit: never make an important decision during an unexpected call, text or email. Hang up, verify the claim independently and involve someone you trust if anything feels off. A scammer needs urgency to win. Taking away that urgency puts you back in control.

item.title: Advocate tells freed Marine vet's physical, psychological torment in Russian prison as 5 Americans remain held
item.description: Global Reach's Kieran Ramsey reveals the beatings and psychological torment Robert Gilman endured during 1,666 days in Russian prison and pleads for remaining detainees.
item.content:encoded:
Kieran Ramsey, the chief investigative officer for Global Reach, detailed the horrific conditions U.S. Marine veteran Robert Gilman experienced while wrongfully detained by Russia and urged the immediate release of five other Americans held in Russia in an interview with Fox News Digital.

Ramsey, who worked with U.S. authorities to secure Gilman's release after 1,666 days in a Russian prison, praised President Donald Trump's efforts to secure Gilman's return on humanitarian grounds.

"Mr. Gilman's home, no doubt, because of the leadership from President Trump. He made a full court press with his senior most team requesting that the Russians release him on a humanitarian basis, which is exactly what happened. And no doubt it was the work of some good, quiet diplomacy on the part of people like Steve Witkoff, his special envoy and Secretary Rubio, and even the CIA director was involved," Ramsey told Fox News Digital.

Gilman was released to U.S. authorities on Tuesday after Russian police arrested him in the city of Voronezh in 2022 after he made an unplanned diversion to Russia on his way to a new teaching job in Moldova. Ramsey detailed the circumstances that led to his arrest.

MARINE VETERAN ROBERT GILMAN RETURNS TO US SOIL AS TRUMP ADMIN FULFILLS REQUEST: 'NO AMERICAN LEFT BEHIND'

"The start of this horrific nightmare comes from the fact that he was actually transiting Moscow. He never intended to stay or visit Russia. He was en route to a new teaching job in Moldova. And while en route, he became really sick. He had to stay and recuperate. And he does have some extended family in Russia. His father had immigrated from Russia years ago. So after he recuperated to where at least he thought he was well enough, he decided to go to the U.S. Embassy in Moscow to renew his passport. But again, en route to the embassy, he became violently ill and that's where Russian police came upon him, thought he was drunk, assaulted him, said that he assaulted them, and then it just snowballed from there," Ramsey revealed.

Ramsey also revealed the treatment Gilman received while in a Russian prison, which included an extensive campaign of beatings and apparent psychological torture.

"Never have we seen the treatment that Mr. Gilman suffered as bad as anybody else. He was provoked in prison. He was beaten in prison, He was forced to exercise, he was forced to fight, and then he was told just some crazy things like, you know, there was a hit team to go assault his father in Boston. And things like that, when they're all together and you're cut off from the outside world and you have no idea if there's any hope, you can imagine how that compounds on somebody," Ramsey explained.

AMERICAN EX-MARINE FEARED NEAR DEATH AFTER WEEKS IN CATATONIC STATE IN RUSSIAN PRISON

When asked if there was any legitimacy to the Boston hit team, Ramsey said "totally psychological mumbo-jumbo disinformation campaign to make him feel awful."

Gilman, Ramsey told Fox News Digital, is now recuperating in a U.S. hospital alongside family, and while he "still has a long road to go," was able to receive immediate medical care thanks, in part, to the State Department designating him as a wrongful detainee.

But Global Reach is representing five other Americans detained in Russia who Ramsey argues also deserve that status and have yet to receive it.

"All five of those we would assert are wrongfully detained do meet the criteria under the Robert Levinson Hostage-Taking and Accountability Act," Ramsey told Fox News Digital, referencing the 2020 bill that grants the president "visa- and property-blocking sanctions against any foreign person responsible for or complicit in the unlawful or wrongful detention of a U.S. national abroad."

FREED MARINE RETURNS HOME 'VERY FRAIL' AFTER RUSSIAN 'NIGHTMARE' AS FAMILY ADVOCATE URGES TRUMP TO FREE OTHERS

But Ramsey also detailed the political hurdles that may prevent the U.S. from immediately recognizing the detainees as wrongfully detained.

"There's been a policy debate inside the State Department as to whether classifying them or categorizing them as wrongfully-detained will raise the price in that diplomacy or that hostage diplomacy negotiations with the Russians to get their release," he explained.

Ramsey then told the stories of his five clients, each facing debilitating health conditions in their imprisonment.

Alexander Antonov, the first of Ramsey's clients he described to Fox News Digital, is an international businessman from California. "He's a proud husband and father. He's an international businessman. He had business interests in Russian-occupied Crimea and Ukraine," Ramsey explained.

Antonov was on his way home from a business trip from Ukraine and transited through Russia "which obviously is a risky venture," Ramsey said.

Russian authorities stopped him and found his U.S. passport and "immediately he became a target for them," Ramsey also said.

Antonov is now sitting in a Russian prison and was recently violently assaulted by another inmate, Ramsey said, adding that he continues to hear reports that Antonov's being harassed simply for being an American.

IRAN JAILS PSYCHOLOGIST OVER TRUMP PLEA AS REGIME DEMANDS HE MAKE AMERICANS ‘LOOK STUPID’: FAMILY

Antonov was detained just over a year ago, Ramsey told Fox News Digital.

He then detailed the case of David Barnes, a Texas native who traveled to Russia to retrieve his children after his Russian ex-wife fled and took them to Russia.

Barnes was embattled in a contentious custody battle with his ex-wife, Ramsey explained, in which she allegedly made unsubstantiated claims about him.

"Mr. Barnes went to Russia to recover his children and his ex-wife yet again made claims of criminality against him and the Russians acted upon it. And he's been sitting in a prison now for over four years, and he's got his own health issues," Ramsey explained.

Olga Jezler, a 36-year-old green card holder who lived in New York, is another detainee Ramsey represents who was taken after flying to Russia to take care of her sick sister.

AMERICAN MISSIONARY KEVIN RIDEOUT RELEASED AFTER MORE THAN 9 MONTHS IN CAPTIVITY IN NIGER

After flying to Russia to take care of her sister with cancer, Russian authorities detained her because she was carrying CBD oil, which Ramsey said was legal in Russia.

"Nevertheless, the Russians saw an opportunity and they charged her with drug trafficking. And today she still sits in a Russian prison," he told Fox News Digital.

Jezler has significant health issues and is at risk of losing her ability to have children, Ramsey said. The condition she has is easily treatable in the U.S., he explained.

Andre Khachatoorian is, Ramsey said, yet another case of somebody who was not supposed to be in Russia.

Khachatoorian was transiting through Russia to reach Armenia while transporting a rifle, Gilman said. He allegedly had all the proper paperwork.

Khachatoorian also has an autoimmune disease that continues to get worse while he been sitting in a Russian prison for more than four years, Ramsey said.

UKRAINE POUNDS BLACK SEA FLEET’S ‘LAST MAJOR STRONGHOLD’ WHILE PUTIN FLEXES NAVAL POWER IN PACIFIC

Ramsey also named Chuck Zimmerman, who Russian authorities nabbed in international waters.

"Chuck Zimmerman is originally from Virginia. He set sail on his lifelong dream with his life savings to sail around the world and end up in New Zealand where he was planning to be a master electrician," Ramsey detailed.

Zimmerman, Ramsey told Fox News Digital, had planned to travel through the Red Sea to reach his final destination, but he rerouted after the war in Iran began.

"He could even hear the bombs from his sailboat where he was at the time. So he decided to divert to the Black Sea. While in the Black Sea, in international waters, the Russian Navy approached him and told him, under threat of force, you will follow us to the Russian port of Sochi or we will sink you," Ramsey told Fox News Digital

Zimmerman had a firearm on board his vessel, leading Russia to charge him with international arms trafficking, Ramsey told Fox News Digital.

He has been in a Russian prison for over a year.

"He has very serious medical issues. We've consulted medical authorities even recently who have told us he either needs to be treated for a bleeding gastric ulcer or perhaps something worse. But at this time, as we sit here, He's unable to eat without having to throw up immediately after. He's losing weight at a very rapid pace. And quite honestly, he's losing hope that he's ever gonna make it out of there," Ramsey said.

RUBIO UNVEILS VISA RESTRICTIONS TARGETING CYBERCRIME NETWORKS

Ramsey again iterated the urgent need for the U.S. to designate his five clients as wrongful detainees.

"We don't want to lose momentum right now," he said.

"Seeing Mr. Gilman come home was fantastic. And I've been asked, 'well, you guys should be, you know patting yourselves on the back or people should be celebrating.' Well, no. It's fantastic. Mr. Gilman's in a hospital in the US with his family right now, but.... We alone have five other families that are going, 'when can we expect the same for our loved one?' And we have to keep the pressure up everywhere we can to make sure people know these folks' names and have an expectation that the U.S. Government is going to do everything they can to convince the Russians to let these people go," he said.

Fox News Digital contacted the U.S. State Department for further comment.

item.title: Harvard research fellow says higher education must rethink what students learn in AI era
item.description: Harvard researcher Christopher Dede argues universities returning to paper tests to prevent AI cheating are missing the point about education.
item.content:encoded:
Higher education is at a crossroads as institutions across the country grapple with how to approach artificial intelligence in the classroom. Universities have instituted policies around the technology, while some professors have returned to paper tests and taken other measures aimed at preventing students from improperly using AI.

However, Harvard University Senior Research Fellow Christopher Dede says they are focusing on the wrong problem, and are not adequately preparing students to face a world in which AI is ubiquitous.

"The problem is that our educational systems are geared to teaching reckoning and their quality is measured by assessing reckoning, the GRE, the SAT, the LSAT, et cetera, et cetera. And so what we're doing is preparing human beings to lose to AI as opposed to preparing human beings with skills that complement AI," Dede told Fox News Digital.

EDUCATORS WARN AI DEBATE HAS FOCUSED TOO MUCH ON CHEATING, NOT ENOUGH ON STUDENT LEARNING

Dede is a seasoned professional when it comes to blending technology and education. He spent 22 years as the Timothy E. Wirth Professor of Learning Technologies at Harvard before becoming a research fellow with the university. Dede also served as the chair of the Learning & Teaching program at Harvard Graduate School of Education from 2001 to 2004.

Central to Dede's view of AI in higher education is the distinction between "reckoning," or calculative prediction, and "judgment." He traces this back to philosopher Brian Cantwell Smith, explaining that while technology is good at reckoning, humans are good at judgment, making the two complementary rather than competitive.

Dede noted that the vast majority of what he has read about AI in education is "about doing things better," such as revamping traditional teaching methods and automating them using generative AI. However, he argued that using AI to teach more efficiently overlooks a larger problem: many of the skills that students can learn from AI are also the ones that the technology will increasingly perform in the workplace.

"It's really important to remember that anything that AI can teach, AI is going to do in the workplace because it's actually much easier to build a workplace tool that just does whatever the skill is than it is to build a teaching tool that somehow has a glass box on top of the black box of AI so that human beings can learn how to do this," he said.

STUDY FINDS MORE AI PRAISE FOR BLACK STUDENTS, SOFTER TREATMENT OF FEMALES

He said that the focus needs to be on "doing better things" rather than simply "doing things better." Dede added that one of the core benefits of using emerging technology in education is actually being able to do something more powerful than what was previously possible.

Dede pointed to active, collaborative and project-based learning, as well as immersive simulations, as ways institutions can use AI to develop students' judgment skills.

He used a negotiations course as an example, saying that a student could take multiple classes on the subject and earn good grades without ever actually demonstrating the ability to successfully negotiate. However, he believes AI could be used to assess whether students actually possess the ability to apply skills they have learned in the classroom.

"So, what AI can do is to mimic the landlord or to mimic a used car dealer or to mimic your boss when you want a raise, and let you rehearse and apply all those wonderful things you learned in your negotiation courses through practice so that when the real world situation comes along, you can give a skilled performance that involves judgment," he said.

Dede argued that generative AI's language capabilities can also help analyze what students say and do during those performances, providing insight into what they retained from the course.

REP. TED LIEU: AI IS ALREADY TOO POWERFUL. WE NEED A KILL SWITCH BEFORE DISASTER STRIKES

As AI becomes increasingly common in professional settings, students will need to learn how to pair the technology's analytical capabilities with human judgment, according to Dede. He said AI assistants can do things that no human realistically could. In his example, he suggested that an AI assistant could examine large quantities of medical literature and draw insights from patient records. However, it also has its limitations, as AI lacks the ability to understand pain and morality or the difference between quantity and quality of life.

"The tools are great for the reckoning part, but they're terrible at the judgment part," Dede told Fox News Digital. He added that professionals could need to be re-skilled so they are able to use AI tools while also recognizing the value of the patterns that the technology picks up.

However, Dede cautions against relying solely on AI for reckoning, saying that students still need to be taught how to reason so the technology does not become "magic." He added that one must be able to discern when an AI tool is spitting out "hallucinatory reckoning" versus "genuine reckoning."

Simply knowing how to use generative AI may not be enough to give students the advantage they seek when entering the workforce.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE OF MEDIA AND CULTURE

One of Dede's colleagues advertised an unpaid internship and received 200 applications from students eager for the opportunity. However, there was a problem. She noticed that the vast majority of applications appeared to be identical as students had put information about the internship into generative AI and told it to write a letter. Dede said his colleague was almost immediately able to eliminate a number of candidates because of her suspicion of AI usage.

The anecdote, according to Dede, illustrates why students need to develop skills to help distinguish themselves from what can be done using AI.

While students need to learn how to use AI without becoming overly dependent on it, Dede argued that restricting the technology in the classroom was not the answer. He said that professors returning to analog methods, such as blue books and paper-only tests in an effort to prevent students from using AI to cheat, are "missing the point entirely."

Dede believes professors in higher education need to ask why they are teaching something, rather than how they can stop students from using technology to cheat.

While he believes it is important for higher education to understand how to teach students to work with AI, Dede is not confident that there will be noticeable changes any time soon.

"I don't know if the elite universities will change, but a lot of the other universities will change in order to survive," he said. "And they'll come out with something that is ultimately far more powerful that's based around demonstrating that their graduates have judgment and understand enough about reckoning that it's non-magic and are capable of thriving on the kind of chaos that we see in the modern world."

Navy SEALs, veterans, first responders and others plunged into the waters of New York Harbor Saturday morning for the annual NYC SEAL Swim, which honors the service and sacrifice of America's greatest heroes.

"This is all about honoring our fallen," retired Navy SEAL Brad Geary told Fox News' Joey Jones. "Honoring our country, honoring God."

Against the backdrop of the Statue of Liberty, Geary joined fellow retired Navy SEALs Bill Brown and Jimmy May to reflect on the mission behind the event, which combines miles of swimming and physical challenges with tributes to those who served and sacrificed.

9/11 MUSEUM CEO REFLECTS ON LASTING IMPACT OF TERROR ATTACKS AS AMERICA MARKS 250TH BIRTHDAY

May, a retired SEAL commander who founded Beyond the Brotherhood, the event's 2026 beneficiary, said the mission for the nonprofit grew out of his own difficult transition from military to civilian life and the loss of four friends to suicide.

item.title: Blue Jays star Vladimir Guerrero Jr gets kneed in the head during chaotic play, leaves game
item.description: Toronto Blue Jays star Vladimir Guerrero Jr. took a knee to the head during a chaotic play at third base, scoring the tying run before being removed from the Blue Jays' win.
item.content:encoded:
Unfortunately for Toronto Blue Jays star Vladimir Guerrero Jr., baseball can sometimes be a contact sport.

In the bottom of the sixth inning during the Blue Jays’ 3-1 win over the New York Yankees on Friday at the Rogers Centre, Guerrero took a knee to the head in a chaotic play.

The Blue Jays were trailing 1-0 with runners on first and second base with one out and George Springer up to bat. Nathan Lukes was on second base, while Guerrero was on first.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE SPORTS COVERAGE ON FOXNEWS.COM

Springer rolled over on Gerrit Cole’s fastball and hit a weak ground ball to third baseman Ryan McMahon. The Yankees’ third baseman charged the ball, stepped on third base, retiring Lukes, and fired to first base to try to complete the inning-ending double play.

Instead, McMahon threw it in the dirt, and first baseman Luis Garcia Jr. was unable to make the catch. When Garcia tried to pick the ball out of the dirt, his glove flew off and the ball went away from him. Guerrero looked to capitalize on the blunder and took off for third base.

Garcia finally recovered, grabbed the ball and fired a bullet to third base. The problem? No one was covering the bag.

Yankees shortstop George Lombard Jr. was a couple of paces off the bag, and Garcia’s throw went into foul territory. As Lombard went to pursue the ill-advised throw, he ran into Guerrero and kneed him in the head, dislodging his helmet.

Despite looking dazed, Guerrero scampered home to tie the game at 1-1. After scoring, he bent over and received help from his teammates as he made his way to the dugout. Guerrero was removed from the game after the collision.

"Kind of precautionary right now," Schneider said of the decision to remove Guerrero. "We'll see how he is tomorrow."

McMahon and Garcia were both charged with errors on the play.

"Just didn't work out, man," McMahon said of the play. "Obviously led to a couple of runs for them and that hurts."

Guerrero, who signed a 14-year, $500 million contract extension with the Blue Jays last season, has had a down year. The six-time All-Star is hitting .263 with just seven home runs and 46 RBI.

The lack of power is astounding, as he has hit at least 23 home runs in every full season of his career. He has not hit a home run at home this year.

While he might not be providing the thump the Blue Jays are used to, he still anchors the middle of their lineup. Losing him would be a significant blow to a Blue Jays team that is in pursuit of the third Wild-Card spot in the American League.
